🔤🔤🔤🔤➖

The Iranian resilience and retaliation appear to have pushed Trump to rely on economic pressure to try to force Iran’s hand. Analysts note that the administration has already imposed extraordinary pain on Iran’s economy, with Trump’s naval blockade compounding the damage done by this spring’s bombing campaign.

A new escalation came on Wednesday when the United Arab Emirates, a crucial economic partner across the Persian Gulf from Iran, said it would halt all trade and financial transactions with the country.

But going further could be difficult for Trump, who warned in his Truth Social post that “ANY country” providing any kind of “lifeline to Iran” would “itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences.”

Iran’s most important financial lifeline is China, which buys most of Iran’s oil.

“China is the indispensable piece” of an economic pressure campaign against Iran, said Miad Maleki, a senior fellow at the hawkish Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank in Washington who previously worked on sanctions policy at the Treasury Department.

“No substitute can absorb Iranian crude at China’s scale,” Maleki added in a text message.

But Trump has worked to improve his relationship with Xi Jinping, the Chinese leader, who is expected to meet Trump in Washington on Sept. 24. 

Analysts said they anticipate that the Trump administration will be cautious in pressuring China, especially given the upcoming summit, leaving open the question of just how much more severe the U.S. economic campaign against Iran can become.

Bessent told CNBC that the administration’s conversations with China on the matter would remain private.

“Iran has been under comprehensive sanctions for years,” said Edward Fishman, senior fellow and director of the Maurice Greenberg Center for Geoeconomics at the Council on Foreign Relations. “The only major thing left to do is aggressively target Iran’s trading partners — above all, China.”

He added: “I’m skeptical Trump is willing to risk instigating an economic war with China right now.”

Then there is the question of how Iran would respond under severe financial strain — especially given the widespread recognition that Trump wants to avoid going back to war.

Ross, the former Mideast envoy, said Iran could be expected to look for a way to put fresh military pressure on the United States or its Gulf allies. And that expectation, in turn, highlights the uncertainty over Trump’s longer-term strategy as gas prices stay high, the midterms loom and munitions stocks remain low.

“I’ve not seen, throughout this process, the ability to think beyond the immediate next step,” Ross said of the administration’s approach to Iran.

💰 Bitcoin is back above $75,000. What changed?

Bitcoin has extended its recovery after breaking above $70,000 for the first time since June.

At the time of publication, BTC is trading near $76,000.

The rally followed several developments:

• the US Treasury announced plans to double buybacks of long-duration government debt
• the move briefly reduced pressure in the bond market and supported risk assets
• President Trump urged Congress to advance the Clarity Act
• a wave of short-covering added momentum to the price increase

Short-covering happens when traders betting on a decline buy Bitcoin to close their positions. That additional demand can accelerate an upward move.

However, this type of forced buying eventually slows down. For the rally to continue, the market will need sustained demand beyond short-covering alone.

A breakout shows momentum.

What happens after the breakout shows whether that momentum is sustainable.

📡 Iran doubles defense weapons production in one year: Defense Ministry spokesperson

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Iran has doubled its production of defense weapons and equipment over the past year, a military official says, emphasizing that strengthening national power is essential to confronting foreign powers seeking to undermine the country’s independence.

Speaking in an interview late on Friday, spokesperson for the Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics, Brigadier General Reza Talaei-Nik, said Iran’s defense industry has become a key pillar of national security and military preparedness. He described the rapid production and replacement of domestically manufactured weapons and ammunition as one of the industry’s main strengths.
​
According to the official, Iran’s defense production capacity has continued to operate alongside the use of weapons and equipment in the field, allowing supplies to be replenished rapidly when needed.
​
Talaei-Nik said defense weapons and equipment production doubled during the past year despite attacks on limited sections of Iran’s defense industry during the 12-day war.
​
He said the country’s ability to maintain a stable supply of weapons and military equipment was among the key factors contributing to its battlefield resilience. This capability, he added, has been supported by cooperation among the Armed Forces, the Ministry of Defense, knowledge-based companies, private-sector firms, and scientific and research centers.
​
Some strategic defense products and wartime supplies experienced more than threefold growth in production during the conflict, the spokesperson noted.
​
Talaei-Nik said Iran’s defense industry has expanded from producing only 31 basic products before the 1979 Islamic Revolution to manufacturing more than 1,000 advanced systems, weapons and ammunition today.
​
He also said that production costs for some Iranian defense systems are up to 20 times lower than those of comparable foreign products.
​
The spokesperson further said Iran managed to withstand the recent conflict despite the United States, the Israeli regime and their supporters having military budgets more than 100 times larger, attributing the outcome to domestic production capabilities and national resilience.
